questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ and let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. Which pair of conditions is equivalent to $H$ being a supporting hyperplane of $V$?
options: $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ (or $\geq b$ for all), and $H\cap V\neq\varnothing$
$\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}<b$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ (or $>b$ for all), and $H\cap\operatorname{Cl}(V)\neq\varnothing$
$\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ (or $\geq b$ for all), and $H\cap\operatorname{Cl}(V)\neq\varnothing$
$\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$, and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq b$ for some $\boldsymbol{y}\notin V$

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, and suppose $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ is a supporting hyperplane of $V$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$, where $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is not constant on $V$. Which formula gives $b$?

Let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ and let $V$ be a nonempty set with $V\subseteq H$, for instance a segment lying in $H$. Is $H$ a supporting hyperplane of $V$?
options: No: a supporting hyperplane meets $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$ in a single point, not in all of $V$
No: $V$ must have at least one point strictly on one side of $H$
Only if $V$ is convex, since supporting hyperplanes are defined for convex sets only
Yes: $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ holds, with equality, on all of $V$, and $V$ meets $H$

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty closed convex set and $\boldsymbol{p}\in\partial V$. Which statement about supporting hyperplanes of $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is correct?
options: There is exactly one, the tangent hyperplane of $V$ at the point $\boldsymbol{p}$
There is at least one, and there can be several, for example at a corner of a polygon
There is one only when $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a corner of $V$, not at smooth boundary points
There may be none at all unless $V$ is also bounded

questions.question: In the graphical method, $Z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ with $(c_1,c_2)\neq(0,0)$ is made as large as possible over a nonempty closed feasible region $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ whose finite optimal value $Z^*$ is attained. How is the final line $\{c_1x_1+c_2x_2=Z^*\}$ related to $F$?
options: It divides $F$ into the points with $Z\leq Z^*$ and those with $Z\geq Z^*$
It passes through an interior point of $F$ where the objective is largest
It supports $F$: $F$ lies in $c_1x_1+c_2x_2\leq Z^*$ and touches the line
It supports $F$ only when the optimal solution is a unique corner of $F$

questions.question: Let $V=[-1,2]\times[0,3]\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$. For which $b$ is $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 2x_1-x_2=b\}$ a supporting hyperplane of $V$ with $2x_1-x_2\leq b$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\leq4,\ x_2\leq3,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,3)$. For which $\boldsymbol{a}$ is the line $\{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}\}$ a supporting hyperplane of $V$ with $V$ on the side $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}$?

Let $V$ be the closed triangle with corners $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$ and $(0,2)$. The line $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2=4\}$ supports $V$ with $x_1+2x_2\leq4$ on $V$. Which set is $H\cap V$?
options: Only the point $(2,1)$ in the middle of an edge

questions.question: Which of these nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ has no supporting hyperplane at all?
Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon |x_1|+|x_2|\leq2\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1)$, a point of $\partial V$. Which line through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a supporting hyperplane of $V$?

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, closed and bounded, and $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. How many $b\in\mathbb{R}$ make $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ a supporting hyperplane of $V$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$?
options: Exactly one, $b=\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in V}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, which exists as $V$ is closed and bounded
Exactly one if $V$ is convex; a nonconvex $V$ may have none for this $\boldsymbol{a}$
One only if $\boldsymbol{a}$ is a normal vector of an edge or face of $V$, otherwise none

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, not necessarily closed, and let $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, be a supporting hyperplane of $V$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ on $V$. Must $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ attain a maximum on $V$?
options: Yes: being supporting provides a point of $V$ on the hyperplane, where $f$ equals $b$
Yes, provided $V$ is convex, since a linear function then reaches its supremum
Yes, provided $V$ is bounded, since the supremum $b$ of $f$ is then finite
No: the value $b$ may be reached only at points of $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$ outside $V$

questions.question: For a nonempty set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with closure $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$, how do the supporting hyperplanes of $V$ compare with those of $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$?
options: $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$ has fewer, as added points of $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$ can lie beyond a hyperplane bounding $V$
They coincide, as a closed halfspace contains $V$ exactly when it contains $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$
$V$ has fewer, as a hyperplane touching only $\operatorname{Cl}(V)\setminus V$ supports $\operatorname{Cl}(V)$ but not $V$
They coincide only when $V$ is convex; for other sets the two families differ

questions.question: Let $V$ be the closed disc with centre $(1,1)$ and radius $5$, $\boldsymbol{p}=(7,9)\notin V$, and $\boldsymbol{q}$ the point of $V$ nearest to $\boldsymbol{p}$. Which line is the hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{q}$ with normal $\boldsymbol{p}-\boldsymbol{q}$, which supports $V$ at $\boldsymbol{q}$?
Let $V$ be the closed triangle with corners $(1,0)$, $(3,2)$ and $(0,4)$. For which values of $b$ is $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2=b\}$ a supporting hyperplane of $V$?

The elliptical region $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+4x_2^2\leq4\}$ lies in $x_1+2x_2\leq b$, and the line $\{x_1+2x_2=b\}$ is a supporting hyperplane of $V$. What is the value of $b$?

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, $\boldsymbol{p}\in\operatorname{Cl}(V)$, and $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which condition on $H$ is equivalent to $H$ being a supporting hyperplane of $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: $V$ lies in one of the two closed halfspaces bounded by $H$
$H$ is a separating hyperplane of $V$ and $\{\boldsymbol{p}\}$
$\boldsymbol{p}\in H$ and $H$ contains no interior point of $V$

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b\}$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, a supporting hyperplane of $V$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b$ on $V$. Can $H$ contain a point of $\operatorname{Int}(V)$?
options: Yes, if $V$ is not convex, since $V$ can then bend back and reach $H$ from inside
Yes, if $V\subseteq H$, since then every point of $V$ lies on the hyperplane $H$
No: near an interior point on $H$ there are points of $V$ beyond $H$
Yes, if $H$ contains a whole edge of $V$, since the midpoint of that edge is interior

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_2\geq\mathrm{e}^{x_1}\}$, a closed convex set. Which horizontal lines $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_2=b\}$ are supporting hyperplanes of $V$?
options: Every $\{x_2=b\}$ with $b\leq0$, since $V$ lies above each of them
Only $\{x_2=1\}$, which passes through the boundary point $(0,1)$
None, since no point of $V$ reaches $\inf_{V}x_2=0$ and $x_2$ is unbounded above

questions.question: Let $V=D_1\cup D_2$, where $D_1$ is the closed disc with centre $(0,0)$ and radius $1$ and $D_2$ is the closed disc with centre $(4,0)$ and radius $2$. Through which of these boundary points of $V$ does a supporting hyperplane of $V$ pass?
